Little can be done to mitigate this noise source; however, the point could be made that the noise duration at any one location will be only a few hours. Also, the ambient noise level for central area streets will be at least 70 dBA. General mitigation measures for construction operations are limited to use of less noisy equipment, particularly trucks and tractors, and careful management of operations to minimize the noise exposure. Typically, construction contracts made by municipal governments specify that the "Standard Specifications" of the State of California which contain noise control regulations be followed.
The final noise impact to be considered results from changes in traffic on the improved streets. In the case of substandard streets, an increase in average speed for automobiles from 15 to 30 MPH would raise noise levels about 3 dBA. For trucks, much less common on residential streets, such a change in speed reduces noise level by about 4 dBA. Neither of these changes in noise levels are readily perceived.
H. URBAN DESIGN
It is assumed that providing loans and funding for rehabilitation and public works improvements can only be positive and beneficial, at least with respect to the physical neighborhood. It is a possibility that, as a secondary effect, the climate of investment will attract new residents.
With respect to the environmental design of these areas, he question of impacts relates to the quality of improvement; i.e. how effectively will the various funds be spent. For example, in the Campus area, will controls be enacted to maintain the existing historical quality of the area, or will ugly apartment blocks continue to be built next to newly-rehabilitated older residences? In Alviso, will the community be provided with an improved park while basements flood and possibly roofs leak. Will the public improvements be designed to respect Mayfair's rural/urban quality? Will a secondary effect of street improvements in Gardner be to strip those neighborhoods of their landscape quality?
To the end of enhancing overall environmental quality, the distribution of funding should be made with some attention to urban design. To what detail these issues should be investigated it is now impossible to say; however it need not be expensive, and its necessity will vary with each project area. But, for instance, there should be some recognition that strict housing code enforcement of older structures may be unwarranted; there would need to be a means of specifying to what degree rehabilitation should occur. Also, the C.D.B.G. Project should respect the idea that there are cultural variations in terms of what makes a good environment.
